sections.h2: Does the city of Peoria send its own property tax bill?
sections.html:
No, the county does. A home within Peoria's limits gets one combined bill spanning the city, the schools and the rest of the taxing bodies on the parcel. The Peoria County Treasurer, who doubles as County Collector, mails it and takes the money. City Hall writes its own rules on registration and transfer tax but never mails a tax bill.

On the county's list of places to pay are the Treasurer, participating banks and township collectors, and the City of Peoria Township Collector is called out separately. Find out which one applies to your parcel before a check goes out.

sections.h2: What is Peoria like, and who buys homes there?
sections.html:
Peoria sits on the Illinois River as seat of Peoria County and anchor of a metro area near 402,000 people. French settlers arrived in 1691, the village was incorporated in 1835 and the city in 1845. In 2020 it counted 113,150 residents, eighth among Illinois cities, on 47.97 square miles of land.

Hospitals drive the local economy. OSF HealthCare has topped the employer list since 2021, with the medical district clustered at Interstate 74 and Knoxville Avenue beside downtown. Caterpillar's headquarters left in 2018, though factories making machinery, metal products and chemicals still matter.

Wikipedia describes cold, snowy winters averaging 26.3 inches of snow, and hot, humid summers.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about Peoria households?
sections.html:
In July 2025 QuickFacts put the city at 110,920 residents, 2.0% below the 2020 base. Just 57.5% of homes are occupied by their owners, against 67.0% countywide, so landlords and tenants figure in many local sales. Median value of an owner-occupied home over 2020-2024 was $156,200.

  • Rent at the median is $1,005 monthly.
  • Households typically earn $59,410, and 21.0% of residents live below the poverty line.
  • Owner costs per month run $1,525 for a mortgage holder and $647 for someone without one.
  • The city counts 49,037 households of 2.20 people on average.
  • The average commute is 17.9 minutes.

These are citywide figures, and individual streets can land far above or below them.

sections.h2: What changed on the 2026 assessment for the City of Peoria Township?
sections.html:
The county's published notice for City of Peoria Township uses a January 1, 2026 valuation date. It sets 33.33% of market value as the target, reports a county median of 31.25%, and draws on sales from 2023 through 2025. One equalization factor, 1.0700, covers the residential, commercial, industrial and farm home site classes.

Owners who doubt a value are told to start with the township assessor at 427 W Main St, Peoria, IL 61606, (309) 324-7459. The Board of Review took complaints June 1 through September 30, 2026, and the notice adds that a filed complaint is what preserves your right to appeal. That period is over and the next begins June 1.

A self-check is printed too: divide your assessment by 33.33%. A result above what the house would fetch suggests it may be over-assessed.

sections.h2: What are the Peoria property tax deadlines?
sections.html:
One bill covers the year and splits into two halves. Halves for the 2025 taxes came due June 9 and September 9, 2026. Payment or postmark on June 10 or September 10 or later brings 1.5% for every month or fraction of one, and the county says there is no grace period.

The sale was scheduled for November 9, 2026. Sold taxes can still be redeemed afterward at the County Clerk, with the buyer's interest and fees.

sections.h2: What city rules touch a Peoria house sale?
sections.html:
Peoria's transfer tax is $2.50 for each $1,000 of value or fraction of $1,000 stated on the transfer declaration, under a 1989 ordinance. It is paid at the Peoria County recording office. If money changes hands on a commercial or multi-family property, the city also wants a zoning certificate dated within the past year, issued by Community Development at 419 Fulton, Room 300, (309) 494-8600.

The city runs a property registration program. Under its FAQ, a home must be registered if it is any of the following:

  • rented to a tenant, including a family member
  • vacant for six months or longer
  • an investment property, meaning not the deeded owner's residence
  • being sold on contract for deed until the deed transfers
  • a multi-family building
  • a short-term rental of 29 days or less
  • in foreclosure

Registration fees are waived for a few cases, including a vacant house listed for sale and a house in probate, though those still have to register. The FAQ shows 2023-2024 fees of $75 for a single-family home, $75 plus $20 per added unit for multi-family, $75 per short-term rental unit with an 8% room tax, and $300 per parcel every six months for foreclosure. Confirm the current amounts with the Office of Accounts Receivable at 419 Fulton Street, Room 100.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid taxes on a Peoria house?
sections.html:
Peoria County sells unpaid taxes in early November. Buyers bid from 0% to 9% interest, and if nobody bids the county takes the parcel at 9% as trustee. Interest is added at the sale and every six months. The owner still holds title during redemption, which defaults to two years and can be stretched to three. For homes of one to six units the county gives a minimum of two and a half years.

Redemption goes to the Peoria County Clerk, 324 Main St, Room 101, in one payment of cash, a cashier's check or a money order. Title company and personal checks are not accepted. A seller in that position should order the Clerk's redemption estimate and share it with the closer.

sections.h2: Which exemptions apply to a Peoria homeowner?
sections.html: The county page lists an owner-occupied exemption of $6,000 off equalized assessed value, a senior exemption of $5,000, a returning veterans exemption of $5,000 and a disabled persons exemption of $2,000. Disabled veterans receive $2,500, $5,000 or a full exemption depending on the service-connected rating. The county's senior deferral program charges 3% and is repaid when the home is sold, so a seller who used it should expect a payoff at closing. Questions go to the Supervisor of Assessments at 309-672-6910.

faqs.q: Does the City of Peoria collect my property tax?
faqs.a: No. The Peoria County Treasurer sends and collects the bill, and taxes can also be paid at participating banks or at the township collector. The city handles registration of rentals, vacant and foreclosure properties and its own transfer tax.

faqs.q: What is the Peoria transfer tax rate?
faqs.a: The city's instruction sheet prints $2.50 for each $1,000 of value or fraction of $1,000 stated on the transfer declaration. It is paid at the Peoria County recording office, and commercial or multi-family transfers need a current zoning certificate.

faqs.q: Does a vacant Peoria house need city registration?
faqs.a: Yes, once it has sat empty six months or more. A vacant house on the market earns a fee waiver but still has to be registered, with proof of the listing, and a house in probate is treated the same way. The Office of Accounts Receivable at City Hall handles it.

faqs.q: When is the Peoria appeal deadline for assessments?
faqs.a: September 30 was the 2026 cutoff, and it is past. Complaints run from June 1 until 30 days after the township publishes changes. Talk to the City of Peoria Township assessor first.

faqs.q: How late can Peoria taxes be paid before the sale?
faqs.a: For 2025 taxes the Treasurer had to receive payment by 5 p.m. on November 6, 2026, and postmarks did not count. The sale was set for November 9, 2026. After a sale, taxes are redeemed through the County Clerk instead.
